preamble: Loss of glottalization in the glottalized palatal approximant (Americanist y̓). In Makah the Proto-Southern-Wakashan glottalized sonorants merged with the plain ones, with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (Davidson 2002: 76, citing Jacobsen 1968), so Nuu-chah-nulth y̓ corresponds to Makah y. Upriver Halkomelem lost resonant glottalization, usually lengthening the preceding vowel, while Island and Downriver keep it (Compton & Gerdts c. 2005): Downriver sqʷəmey̓, Upriver sqwemá:y 'dog'. For the Chimakuan languages, the correspondence table in Wikipedia's Chimakuan languages article (after Powell 1974) gives the reflexes of the glottalized resonants as R or ʔR, *y̓ appearing in Quileute as y or ʔy. Quileute words given elsewhere in the article, such as káʔyis 'aunt' and the numeral báʔyas 'four', show a glottal stop followed by a plain y, so the glottalization may survive as a separate segment rather than be lost; they are not listed as examples here. According to the same table, Chemakum instead hardened *y̓ to (ʔ)č.

languageExamples.context: Davidson (2002: 76): the Proto-Southern-Wakashan glottalized sonorants merged with the plain sonorants in Makah, with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (citing Jacobsen 1968); Nuu-chah-nulth keeps them. Werle (2010: 4) lists the "loss of glottalized resonants in Makah with concomitant lengthening of a preceding vowel"

examples.note: Davidson (2002: 76), ex. (127), beside Nuu-chah-nulth ʔ̴uy̓i; Werle (2010: 7), ex. (15), writes Makah q̓uˑy. Proto-Nootkan form after Fortescue (2007), from the Wiktionary appendix of Proto-Wakashan reconstructions, which lists no descendants; it writes glottalized resonants with a vertical stroke (y̍) where Davidson and Werle write y̓. The long u· before y is the compensatory lengthening. Davidson writes the Nuu-chah-nulth pharyngealized glottal stop as ʔ̴: the initial *q̓ is kept in Makah but became ʔ̴ in Nuu-chah-nulth (Davidson 2002: 75, ex. (126), after Jacobsen 1969a).
Davidson (2002: 366), suffix list, beside Nuu-chah-nulth -y̓a· 'troubled by, with ...'. Proto-Nootkan form after Fortescue (2007), Wiktionary appendix.
Werle (2010: 4), ex. (5), beside Nuu-chah-nulth wiiy̓a and Ditidaht wiiy̓, which keep the glottalization. Proto-Nootkan form after Fortescue (2007), Wiktionary appendix.

languageExamples.language: Downriver Halkomelem y̓ ~ Upriver Halkomelem y (correspondence)
languageExamples.context: Compton & Gerdts (c. 2005), on Upriver: "glottalized resonants have lost their glottalization, usually lengthening the preceding vowel"; Island and Downriver keep them

examples.to: Upriver sqwemá:y 'dog raised for its wool'
examples.note: Wiktionary (sqwemá:y) lists sqʷəmey̓ as an alternative form with the qualifier Hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓, which Wikipedia gives as the name of the Downriver dialect. The headword carries no dialect label, but the page cites Galloway's Dictionary of Upriver Halkomelem (2009). No Proto-Salish or Proto-Central Salish form of the word was found online. The page also lists the cognates Squamish sḵwemáy̓ and Klallam sqʷəmə́y̕. A possible second example is Upriver sch'i:ye 'strawberry (fruit)' beside Downriver sc'iy'e, but the Upriver plant name sch'iy'e:lhp is still written with y' (Compton & Gerdts).
